title: Spread Zeros to Row and Column
statement:
You get a grid grid of integers with m rows and n columns. For every cell that holds 0 in the original grid, set its whole row and its whole column to 0.

Zeros you write while doing this do not spread further. Change grid in place and return nothing. An O(m + n) memory answer is easy; aim for O(1) extra memory.

examples.why: One zero clears row 0 and column 1. If the new zeros in row 0 spread too, the whole grid would become 0.
Two original zeros, each clearing a row and a column. Cells 1 and 3 in the top row survive: no original zero shares their row or column.
The zero sits in the corner where the O(1) trick keeps its flags. Clear row 0 too early and every column looks flagged, so 7 and 9 are wrongly wiped.

hints: First find which rows and which columns must end up zero, and only then write. Writing while you scan lets new zeros spread.
Two boolean arrays, one per row and one per column, are enough. Can the grid store those flags itself?
Use the first row as the column flags and the first column as the row flags. Remember separately whether the first row and first column had a zero of their own, and clear them last.

explain.intuition:
The trap is doing it in one pass: as soon as you write a zero, later cells cannot tell an original zero from a new one, and zeros spread across the whole grid. So split the job: first record which rows and columns must be cleared, then clear them. Two boolean arrays of length m and n do the recording in O(m + n) memory.

For O(1) memory, reuse the grid. Row 0 already has one cell per column, and column 0 has one cell per row, so they can hold the flags: when grid[i][j] is 0, write 0 into grid[i][0] and grid[0][j]. Those cells are going to be zero anyway, so nothing real is lost. The one catch: the flags overwrite row 0 and column 0, so first remember in two plain booleans whether row 0 or column 0 had a zero of its own. Clear the inner cells from the flags, and handle row 0 and column 0 last, after their flags have been read.
steps: Set rowZero if row 0 contains a 0 and colZero if column 0 contains a 0.
For every cell with i ≥ 1 and j ≥ 1 that is 0, set grid[i][0] = 0 and grid[0][j] = 0.
For every cell with i ≥ 1 and j ≥ 1, set it to 0 if grid[i][0] or grid[0][j] is 0.
If rowZero, clear row 0. If colZero, clear column 0.
pitfalls: Clearing rows and columns as soon as you meet a zero. The new zeros then look original and wipe out everything after them.
Clearing row 0 or column 0 before the inner cells. The flags they hold are gone before you use them.
Using grid[0][0] as the flag for both row 0 and column 0. A zero elsewhere in row 0 would then also clear column 0: [[2, 0, 4], [5, 6, 7], [8, 9, 1]] would wrongly lose 5 and 8.

solutions.title: Row and column flag arrays
solutions.idea: Scan once to mark which rows and columns contain a zero, then scan again and zero every cell whose row or column is marked.

solutions.title: First row and column as markers
solutions.idea: Store the column flags in row 0 and the row flags in column 0. Two booleans remember whether row 0 and column 0 must be cleared themselves.

followups: The grid is a huge sparse matrix stored as a list of non-zero cells. How do you apply the same rule?
Instead of zeroing, each original zero should clear only the cells in its row and column within distance k. What changes?
Can you do the O(1) version with a single extra boolean instead of two?
